from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

    text=p.extract_text()

Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i} ===\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1)))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()[:42000])
PY"

strengths: Addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: determining whether brain-to-text decoding scores reflect information recovered from cognitive signals or memorization of text stimuli.

Examines five splitting strategies across EEG and fMRI using public datasets and established decoding models. Tables 2–3 demonstrate substantial sensitivity to the evaluation protocol, supporting the need for more explicit generalization targets.

The proposed joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is well motivated for evaluating transfer to unseen subjects reading unseen text. Grouping fMRI data by story addresses overlapping windows, and the paper acknowledges the resulting data-retention tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence (Section 4.4). Decreasing validation loss does not establish encoder degradation, and improving test scores with longer training does not establish decoder memorization. A randomly initialized encoder still processes cognitive signals; random initialization alone is not a control for their contribution. Real-signal, shuffled-signal, and signal-free comparisons are needed to support the claim that accurate generation occurs without useful brain information.

The experiments do not isolate the amount of performance inflation attributable to overlap. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together. Splitting strategies also change subject and stimulus distributions, while retained training sizes are unreported. Comparisons with matched optimization and data budgets, independently varying subject and stimulus overlap, would make the attribution substantially stronger.

The supplied algorithms do not guarantee the advertised disjointness as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks whether a subject is held out but does not prevent adding an edge to a held-out text. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks task membership but does not exclude held-out subjects. These edge-restoration steps can reintroduce precisely the overlap the method promises to eliminate. The specification needs correction and verification of pairwise subject and stimulus disjointness.

The leakage metrics and reported scores contain substantive inconsistencies. Equation 7 uses an intersection of recordings to represent subject overlap, although distinct recordings from the same subject need not intersect; its denominator is also zero for entirely held-out subjects. Table 1 therefore cannot be reproduced unambiguously from the definition. Separately, Table 3 reports ROUGE-1 F = 84.64 with precision = 63.16 and recall = 71.50, which is incompatible with standard, consistently aggregated F1. The definitions and calculations require an audit.

The blanket characterization of prior splitting methods as contaminated needs qualification. Subject overlap can be appropriate for evaluating a calibrated, within-subject decoder on unseen text. The paper's joint-transfer objective is legitimate, but criticism of previous evaluations should depend on the generalization claims those evaluations actually make.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claimed benchmark release. The manuscript provides no repository or split-file link, exact partition assignments, filtered and retained sample counts, or complete inference protocol, including whether reference prefixes are supplied during evaluation. Four seeds are reported for leakage rates, but decoding results lack variability estimates across splits or training runs. Correcting the specification and providing controlled, repeatable evaluations are necessary before a Findings recommendation; the useful core supports revision next cycle.
